newsitem.title: UK: World refinery margins slip but still running strong.
newsitem.headline: World refinery margins slip but still running strong.

text.p: Refinery profit margins retreated last week but refiners are still enjoying the healthiest rewards for processing oil since last year.
Once again refinery complexes in Asia led the charge, boosted by good regional demand and high world prices for oil products.
But a complex Singapore refinery running Dubai crude was making 50 cents less a barrel this week than last according to Reuters calculations using standard product yields.
A typical complex Asian refinery averaged a profit of $5.51 a barrel last week, with strong demand for gas oil and gasoline there supporting profitability in other regions, notably the Mediterranean.
The mild price recovery in crude, which has been boosted by demand from refiners keen to profit from better margins, has started to force margins off their highs, traders say.
Plants in Europe, the Mediterranean and the United States have all seen sharp falls from early month margin peaks.

A less sophisticated, hydroskimming refinery in Europe is once again earning less than a $1 a barrel ($0.81), half of its peak profitability in early-April, but still well above parlous early year lows.
A complex European refinery averaged returns of $2.44 a barrel last week, off 18 cents on the week, but still well ahead of a three week period in Febuary and March where margins were less than a $1.

Slim profits earlier in the year forced many European refiners to cut throughputs. That, and a heavy maintenance programme, left markets hungry for products when better profits prompted refineries to crank back up.
But maximised production may soon begin to weigh markets with unwanted output, some traders said.
"It could be we are at the end of the refinery bull run. We have to see how product demand holds up and that's still led by Asia," said one trader.

"There are good margins especially on high sulphur fuel but refiners are running at full capacity and that will flood the market at some stage soon. My impression is the market will come off in three weeks time," another dealer said.

In the Mediterranean margins averaged $1.69 last week for a simple refinery running Urals crude. Tuesday's figure was a much lower $1.04 but producers said they would wait for the week's pattern to unfold before crying doom.

Profits for U.S. refineries running key domestic grade West Texas Intermediate (WTI) averaged $1.28, well above average losses of nearly $1 a barrel last September but under highs of well over $2 a barrel in November.

Brent's return averaged $2.75 a barrel in the U.S. last week, and stood at $2.14 yesterday, with Gulf and Atlantic coast appetite for the North Sea blend strong. -- Sean Maguire, London newsroom +44 171 542 8060
